## Overview

The nicheR Shiny app is a point-and-click interface to the functions
documented in the other vignettes. It walks you through four steps: building
an ellipsoid, predicting it onto a study area, adding sampling bias, and
generating virtual data. Nothing in the app is required to use the
package, but it is useful for exploring parameter choices before writing a
script, and for building several competing ellipsoids and comparing them side
by side.

This vignette describes the interface. It does not repeat the theory or the
argument-by-argument detail of the underlying functions, which is covered
elsewhere. Each section points to the vignette that does cover it, and the
links work both in the installed vignettes and on the
[package website](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/).

Launch the app with:

```{r}
library(nicheR)
run_gui()
```

### Where each control comes from

| App page | Package functions | Where the details are |
|---|---|---|
| Build, ranges | `ranges_from_data()`, `ranges_from_stats()` | [Building ellipsoids](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/creating_ellipsoid_based_niches.html) |
| Build, ellipsoid | `build_ellipsoid()` | [Building ellipsoids](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/creating_ellipsoid_based_niches.html) |
| Build, covariance and centroid | `update_ellipsoid_covariance()`, `update_ellipsoid_centroid()` | [Building ellipsoids](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/creating_ellipsoid_based_niches.html) |
| Predict | `predict()` | [Predictions](predict.html) |
| Bias | `prepare_bias()`, `apply_bias()` | [Sampling bias data](bias.html) |
| Generate, from a surface | `sample_data()`, `sample_biased_data()` | [Generate data](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/generating_data.html) |
| Generate, virtual mode | `virtual_data()` | [Generate data](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/generating_data.html) |
| Every plot tab | `plot_ellipsoid()`, `plot_ellipsoid_pairs()`, `add_ellipsoid()`, `add_data()` | [Visualization](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/plotting_vignette.html) |

Two things the app does not do are multi-species communities
(`random_ellipses()`, `nested_ellipses()`, `conserved_ellipses()`) and
scripted batch runs. For those, see the
[Virtual community simulation](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/virtual_communities.html) vignette and work in
the console.

## The About page

The app opens on the About page. Each of the four numbered boxes describes one
step of the workflow and links to the matching package vignette. The sidebar on
the left is how you move between steps once you have started.


<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide1.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

Two buttons sit in the header and are available from every page:

- **Save** writes your current progress to an `.rds` file. You can reload it
  later from the Previous session input option.
- **Report** writes an `.Rmd` script that describes and reproduces the
  current session.

Click **START** at the bottom of the About page to move to step 1.

<br>

# Step 1: Build

## Providing data

The Build page opens on the **Inputs** tab. Start by choosing one of four ways
to supply your environmental data. Switching to a different input type later
starts the session over. Once you have confirmed variables or built an
ellipsoid, the app asks before doing so.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: Inputs tab, input type radio buttons -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide2.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

**Background layers.** Upload either one or more rasters (`.tif` or `.rds`, up
to ten files) or a single CSV describing the environmental conditions of your
study area. The two are alternatives, not a pair: as soon as you select one the
other is hidden, and **Clear files** brings both back.

A raster always supports both environmental space and geographic space. A CSV
supports geographic space only if it carries coordinate columns that fall on a
regular grid, in which case the app converts it to a raster for you. Coordinate
columns are recognized by name (`x`, `lon`, `longitude`, `easting` paired with
`y`, `lat`, `latitude`, `northing`) and are excluded from the variables you can
model. If no coordinates are present, or the points are scattered rather than
gridded, the app warns you and continues in environmental space only.

That restriction follows the package: `predict()` accepts both `SpatRaster` and
`data.frame` inputs and returns a matching type, so a coordinate-free table
still gives you suitability values, but there is no geography to map them onto.
The Build and Predict pages work as normal, and the geographic plots and the
Bias page are unavailable.

**Previous session.** Load an `.rds` file saved earlier with the Save button in
the header. The app resumes where you left off, including confirmed variables,
every saved ellipsoid, and their lineage.

**Virtual mode.** Work entirely in environmental space with no geographic
coordinates. You name the variables and define their ranges directly. Use this
when you are simulating a niche rather than modeling a real study area.
Virtual mode skips steps 2 and 3 and takes you straight to Generate, since
there is nothing to project onto and nothing to bias.

**Example data.** Use the WorldClim bioclimatic layers for Central America
bundled with nicheR, which also includes bias layers for step 3. This is the
fastest way to see the whole workflow.

```{r}
# The example data the app loads
bios <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "ma_bios.tif", package = "nicheR"))
```

<br>

## Selecting variables

Between two and six variables can be used at once. Each row has a checkbox and a
dropdown: uncheck a row to exclude that variable, and use the dropdown to
change which layer occupies that slot. A variable already chosen in one active
slot is removed from the other dropdowns, so you cannot select the same layer
twice. The plot beside the controls updates as you choose, before you confirm
anything.

In virtual mode you instead choose how many dimensions you want, from two to
six, and type a name for each. Blank names default to `var1`, `var2`, and so on. Names can use
letters, numbers, and underscores, and must start with a letter.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: variable selectors with three slots, one unchecked -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide3.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

Click **Confirm** to lock in the selection. The box collapses to a summary with
an **Edit variables** link. If you have not built an ellipsoid yet, editing
simply reopens the selectors. If you have, the app warns you first: editing
clears the ellipsoid, the ranges, and everything downstream.

## Setting ranges

Ranges define the extent of the ellipsoid along each variable. `build_ellipsoid()`
turns a two-row data frame of minima and maxima into a centroid, a covariance
matrix, semi-axis lengths, and a niche volume. The three methods below are three
ways of filling in that data frame. You can switch methods and change values
freely until you build the ellipsoid. After that the ranges are fixed, and a
different set of ranges means a new ellipsoid.

**Manual** lets you type a minimum and maximum for each variable. Defaults come
from the first and third quartiles of your background data.

**From Data** takes a CSV of records for your species, or any table with one column
per selected variable, and uses the observed minimum and maximum of each.
Column names must match your selected variables exactly. Once matched, the
observed bounds appear along with **Expand min** and **Expand max** fields that
widen the ranges outward by a percentage. Negative values shrink them. This is
`ranges_from_data()`.

**From Stats** builds ranges from a mean and standard deviation per variable,
combined with a confidence level. Defaults are derived from your background
data, but you can replace them with published values for your species. This is
`ranges_from_stats()`, and it is the option to use when you know a species'
tolerances but have no records for it, which is the usual situation for
rare species.

> The choice between these methods, and what the confidence level does to the
> resulting ellipsoid, is discussed in the
> [Building ellipsoids](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/creating_ellipsoid_based_niches.html) vignette.

<!-- SCREENSHOT (retake): From Stats panel with three variables, showing the
Ellipsoid confidence level box above the range methods -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide5.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

The range lines on the plot follow whatever you type, so you can preview a
range before committing to it. Once an ellipsoid exists, the lines show the
ranges it was built from and stay there, even if you move the centroid. In
virtual mode there is no background data to anchor the plot, so the plot keeps
a fixed frame around those ranges and the lines hold still while the ellipsoid
moves.

**Reset to defaults** restores the starting values for the current method.
**Initialize Ellipsoid** builds the ellipsoid and unlocks the Covariance and
Centroid sections. From then on the Ranges box shows the ranges as a read-only
table. To use different ranges, click **Create new ellipsoid** at the bottom of
the [ellipsoid library](#the-ellipsoid-library).

The Ranges box also holds the **Ellipsoid confidence level**, which sets where
the boundary of the ellipsoid falls. A higher value draws a larger ellipsoid
around the same centroid. It stays editable after the ellipsoid is built and
applies right away. This is a different number from the confidence level in
From Stats, which only sets how wide the ranges are.

<!-- SCREENSHOT (retake): Ranges box after Initialize Ellipsoid, showing the
read-only range table -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide6.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

## Covariance

A newly built ellipsoid is axis-aligned: every covariance is zero. Adjusting a
covariance rotates the ellipsoid in the plane of that variable pair, which is
how you represent correlated tolerances. A species whose upper temperature
tolerance depends on available moisture does not occupy a box, and the rotation
is what expresses that.

One slider appears per pair, so three variables give three sliders, four give
six, and so on. Slider limits are computed so the covariance matrix stays
positive definite, and moving one slider narrows the range available to the
others. If a combination would be invalid the app shows an error and leaves the
value unchanged. The rotate icon beside each slider resets that pair to zero,
and **Reset all to zero** returns to the axis-aligned form.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: covariance sliders for a three-variable ellipsoid -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide7.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

Click **Set Covariances** when you are satisfied. The section collapses, and
**Edit covariances** reopens it.

> `update_ellipsoid_covariance()` does the same thing from the console, and the
> [Building ellipsoids](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/creating_ellipsoid_based_niches.html) vignette shows how
> rotation changes niche volume and overlap.

## Moving the centroid

The centroid mover shifts the ellipsoid through environmental space without
changing its shape, size, or orientation. Use it to ask what happens if a
species occupies the same breadth of conditions centered somewhere else. This is
`update_ellipsoid_centroid()`.

**Reset all** returns the centroid to where this ellipsoid started. For a copy,
that is the centroid of the ellipsoid it was copied from. For an ellipsoid built
from its own ranges, it is the center of those ranges.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: centroid sliders with one shifted -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide8.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

## The ellipsoid library

The library lists every version you have saved. The highlighted row at the top
is the **working** ellipsoid, the one the plots and every later tab use. Its
label shows whether you are editing or viewing it.

<!-- SCREENSHOT (retake): ellipsoid library with three saved versions, showing
the five row actions and Create new ellipsoid at the bottom -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide9.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

Each saved row has five actions:

- **View** loads the version read-only. Ranges, covariances, and the centroid
  are shown but locked, so you can inspect a version without changing it.
  The **Edit** button on the working row unlocks it.
- **Edit** loads the version with its covariances, centroid, and confidence
  level editable. The ranges stay as they were built. **Update** then
  overwrites that version in place. If the version already has predictions,
  biased layers, or record sets, the app asks first: those were made from
  the previous shape, so updating removes them.
- **Add** creates a new unsaved copy, carrying over the covariance, centroid,
  and ranges of the version you copied from.
- **Export** saves the version to an `.rds` file with `save_nicheR()`, which
  you can read back in the console with `read_nicheR()`.
- **Delete** removes the version and everything derived from it.

**Save** stores the working version under a name of your choice. If the working
version is already in the library the button reads **Update** and overwrites
it.

**Create new ellipsoid**, at the bottom of the library, empties the working
slot and takes you back to the variables and the range methods, so you can
build another ellipsoid from different ranges. Saved versions stay in the
library. If the working version has changes you have not saved, the app asks
before discarding them. **Continue** asks the same question before moving to
the next step.

### Lineage

The **Details** column records where each ellipsoid came from. A copy shows
the name of its parent; an ellipsoid built directly from ranges shows **root**.

Lineage follows the ranges. An ellipsoid built from its own ranges is always a
root, because new ranges describe a different ellipsoid. A copy keeps the
ranges of its parent, and changing its covariance or centroid keeps the lineage
intact.

Deleting a parent does not delete its copies. They are kept and become roots
themselves, and the app tells you how many will be affected before you confirm.

## The Build plots

Three tabs sit beside the controls.

**E-space** shows your background data in environmental space with the ellipsoid
drawn over it. The **Pairs** view gives one panel per variable pair; the **2D**
view gives one large panel for two variables you choose. These are the app's
versions of `plot_ellipsoid_pairs()` and `plot_ellipsoid()`.

**G-space** shows the study area geographically. Before an ellipsoid exists it
shows which cells fall inside your current ranges, one map per variable,
updating as you edit the ranges. Once an ellipsoid exists it switches to the
suitable area. The **Show** control lets you move between the two.

**Combined** places an E-space panel beside a G-space panel.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: E-space pairs view with an ellipsoid -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide10.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

Every plot has an **Advanced Plot Settings** panel below it controlling point
shapes, sizes, and colors, and an **Export figure** button that writes PNG,
PDF, or SVG at a size you specify. The default is a 166 x 166 mm full-page
publication figure.

<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide11.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

> The exported figures are produced by the same base R plotting functions you
> would call yourself. If you need a layout the app does not offer, the
> [Visualization](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/plotting_vignette.html) vignette covers the full set of
> arguments.

Click **Continue** to move to Prediction.

<br>

# Step 2: Predict

Prediction projects a saved ellipsoid onto your background data to produce
suitability surfaces.

<!-- SCREENSHOT (retake): Predict controls, with the truncation box open -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide12.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

**Ellipsoid Version** chooses what to predict. Pick **All versions** to predict
every saved ellipsoid in one pass, or a specific one. Choosing a specific
version also loads it into the working slot, so the plots switch to show it.

**Output layers** are four checkboxes, matching the four outputs of `predict()`:

- **Suitability**, a continuous surface, highest at the centroid and decreasing
  toward the boundary
- **Suitability truncated**, the same surface with everything outside the
  ellipsoid's confidence boundary set to zero
- **Mahalanobis**, distance from the centroid
- **Mahalanobis truncated**, the same, set to `NA` outside the ellipsoid

At least one must be selected. When you switch between saved ellipsoids the
checkboxes update to show which layers that version has already predicted.

Each run replaces the previous prediction for that ellipsoid. It does not add
to it, so to keep several layers, select all of them and predict once.

The difference between the truncated and untruncated forms matters more than it
looks, because it decides what step 4 can sample from. A truncated layer has a
hard niche boundary; an untruncated one does not.

> The [Predictions](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/predict.html) vignette works through the four outputs, the
> truncation logic, and how raster and data frame inputs differ.

**Advanced prediction settings** holds a truncation level that overrides the
ellipsoid's own confidence level, letting you truncate the prediction inward
without rebuilding. The box starts at the confidence level of the ellipsoid you
selected, and leaving it unchanged or blank means no adjustment. With **All
versions** selected it starts empty, since each ellipsoid has its own level.

Predictions are stored per ellipsoid, so predicting one version never discards
another's results. Re-predicting a version clears any biased surfaces and
records derived from the old prediction, since those would otherwise be
stale.

Once a version is predicted, the download icon on its row in the library saves
the prediction. You choose which layers to include, whether to add the
environmental variables, and the format: a raster (`.tif`) or a table (`.csv`)
with the `x` and `y` coordinates. Only layers from the last prediction are
listed.

<!-- SCREENSHOT (retake): Predict library with the download icon -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide13.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

## The Predict plots

**E-space** works like the Build tab, with an added overlay selector once a
prediction exists. Choose a layer to color the background points by its values,
or **Binary suitability** to highlight only the suitable points. The **2D** view
ignores the selector and gives one panel per predicted layer. The coloring is
`add_data()`.

**G-space** shows one map per predicted layer, or a single suitable-area map
when you switch **Show** to the binary view. Before you predict, it previews the
suitable area from the ellipsoid alone.

**Combined** lets each side choose independently. Tick several layers for either
side and the panels subdivide within their column, so the E-space column keeps
its width no matter how many maps you show.

Continuous layers use a viridis palette by default, changeable and reversible in
the settings panel.

<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide14.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

<!-- SCREENSHOT: -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide15.png'

# Step 3: Bias (optional)

Sampling bias weights data generation toward areas with more detection
effort. It describes where people looked, not where the species can live, and
the two are kept separate throughout. This whole step is optional: **Skip bias**
at the top moves straight to Generate, and records will be sampled from the
unbiased prediction.

<!-- SCREENSHOT (retake): Bias controls, with Add new bias layer and the download
icon in the library -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide16.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

**Upload** one or more rasters representing sampling effort: road density,
distance to water, urbanization, collector coverage, anything that stands in for
detection probability. With the example dataset, an **Example bias** button loads
the bundled layers.

**Prepare** assigns each layer a direction and combines them into one composite
surface. *Direct* means higher values increase sampling probability; *inverse*
means they decrease it. Behind the button, `prepare_bias()` rescales every layer
to [0, 1], applies the direction, and combines them. The NA handling control
decides whether the composite keeps pixels valid in any layer (union) or only
those valid in every layer (intersection). The formula used is shown once
prepared.

**Apply** weights a prediction by the composite surface. Choose which ellipsoid
and which prediction layer, and whether the effect is direct or inverse. **All
prediction layers** applies the bias to every layer `predict()` produced for
that ellipsoid. Combinations that already exist are skipped, so you can keep
adding without losing what is applied. Note that once bias has been applied the
result is no longer a probability, which is why step 4 samples biased layers
with a different function.

After the first application the Apply box collapses to a summary. To bias
another layer or another ellipsoid, click **Add new bias layer** at the bottom
of the ellipsoid library, which reopens the box. **Done** closes it again.

Re-preparing the surface clears everything applied from the old one, along with
any record sets generated from those biased layers, since those results no
longer match.

Once bias is prepared, the download icon on each row of the library saves the
bias layers. You choose among the composite surface, the individual prepared
layers, and the biased predictions for that ellipsoid, and the format: a raster
(`.tif`) or a table (`.csv`) with the `x` and `y` coordinates. The composite and
the prepared layers are the same for every ellipsoid. If they sit on a different
grid than the biased predictions, the two groups are downloaded separately.

> The [Sampling bias data](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/bias.html) vignette covers how directions interact,
> what the composite formula does, and how to choose layers that represent
> effort rather than habitat.

## The Bias plots

**Bias layers** shows each raw layer beside its processed version once prepared.
**Composite** shows the combined surface. **Prediction comparison** shows the
unbiased prediction beside every biased version of that layer, so the effect of
the bias is visible directly. Pick the prediction layer to compare from the
dropdown above the maps. Applying bias jumps you to that tab automatically.

<!-- SCREENSHOT: -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide17.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

# Step 4: Generate

The final step draws virtual records. Which controls you see depends
on how you started, because the app calls a different function in each case.

| How you started | Function used | Points carry |
|---|---|---|
| Prediction, no bias applied | `sample_data()` | coordinates or environmental values only |
| Prediction with bias applied | `sample_biased_data()` | coordinates |
| Virtual mode | `virtual_data()` | environmental values only |

<!-- SCREENSHOT (retake): Generate controls, with the unbiased and biased surface columns -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide18.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

<br> 

## Sampling from a prediction

**Number of points** sets how many points to draw, and **Random seed** makes
the draw reproducible. The same seed with the same settings reproduces the same
records; change it to draw a different replicate.

**Surface** lists every available prediction layer as a checkbox. You can select
several at once and get one record set per layer. If bias has been applied,
the list splits into two columns separated by a line, with the unbiased layers
on the left and the biased layers, in orange, on the right. Selecting a layer
from each side is how you compare what bias did to your sample.

**Sampling strategy** sits under the unbiased layers, because it only applies to
them. It controls where the points fall within the niche. *Centroid* weights
toward the niche center, *edge* toward the boundary, and *random* samples evenly
across all suitable cells. The centroid and edge options are what let you
simulate species that are common at their optimum versus those detected mostly
at their margins. The strategies are checkboxes, so you can select more than one
and get a set for each, all with the same number of points and the same seed.
The app reports which weighting method it will use, `suitability` or
`mahalanobis`, inferred from the layer names.

Biased layers are sampled with `sample_biased_data()`, which takes no sampling
strategy and no method. The weights are already in the surface, so a strategy
argument would double-count them. This is why no strategy is offered on the
biased side. When you select a biased layer the app reports its method as bias
weighted, and that is how those sets are labeled afterwards.

**Strict filtering** removes NA and zero-valued cells before sampling.
Recommended for truncated layers, where zero means "outside the niche" rather
than "very low suitability". It applies to unbiased and biased layers alike.

**Advanced settings** holds an optional sampling mask, restricting generation to
a specific area.

In a session built on a table with no usable grid, the prediction is a table
too, and the points are rows drawn from it. They carry the environmental
values, plus the coordinate columns if the table has them. A sampling mask needs
a raster, so it is not offered there.

> The [Generate data](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/generating_data.html) vignette covers the
> strategies and weighting methods in full, including what strict mode does when
> a surface has no zeros.

## Sampling in virtual mode

Virtual mode has no prediction surface and no geography, so the controls are
different. Points are drawn from the multivariate normal defined by the
ellipsoid's centroid and covariance, using `virtual_data()`.

**Number of points** and **Random seed** work as above.

**Truncate to the ellipsoid** decides whether points are constrained inside the
confidence boundary. With truncation off, the tails of the distribution extend
past it.

**Point distribution** chooses how density varies inside the ellipsoid.
*Centroid* concentrates points near the centroid, *edge* concentrates them near
the boundary, and *random* spreads them evenly through the volume. These are the
`direct`, `inverse`, and `uniform` effects of `virtual_data()`. Edge and random
both require truncation, so they only appear when truncation is on.

The result is a table of environmental values with no coordinates. Environmental
space plots work as usual; geographic plots are unavailable, and the app tells
you so rather than drawing an empty map.

## Record sets

Each run produces one set per layer and sampling strategy, and sets accumulate
rather than replace. Changing any parameter, the seed included, gives you a new
set alongside the old one, so a sample-size or seed series builds up in one
place.

The **Record sets** panel lists them with an eye icon each. Toggling the eye
controls which sets the plots draw, up to four at a time per ellipsoid. In the
pairs view all visible sets are overlaid and color-coded with a shared legend;
in the 2D and combined views each set gets its own panel.

Each set is labeled with its layer, plus whichever settings differ between the
sets you have, so a series that differs only by seed reads as the layer and the
seed. Sets drawn from a biased layer are labeled bias weighted. Virtual sets
always show the sampling and whether they were truncated, since they have no
layer name to carry that.

Records are stored per ellipsoid, and the library shows how many each has
produced. You can download one set, every set for the working ellipsoid, or
everything. Every download is a CSV whose first columns identify the set:
`ell_id`, `ell_name`, `layer`, `n`, `seed`, and `sampling`, followed by
`strict` for sets drawn from a surface or `truncate` for virtual sets.

# Working with several ellipsoids

The library, lineage, and per-ellipsoid storage exist so you can carry more than
one hypothesis through the whole workflow at once.

A typical use: build an ellipsoid from published tolerances, build a second one
from wider ranges to represent uncertainty in those tolerances, and copy the
first with a rotated covariance to represent correlated variables. Predict all three
in one pass, apply the same bias surface to all three, and generate records
from each. The **Details** column keeps track of which came from which, and
every plot tab lets you switch between them without losing anything.

Save the session at any point and the whole structure, including lineage, comes
back when you reload it.

This is a hand-built version of what the community functions do
programmatically. If your ellipsoids differ by a rule rather than by hand,
`random_ellipses()`, `nested_ellipses()`, and `conserved_ellipses()` generate
them for you and scale past the handful the library is designed for. See the
[Virtual community simulation](https://castanedam.github.io/nicheR/articles/virtual_communities.html) vignette.

<br>

# The session report

The **Report** button in the header writes a summary of the session as it
stands. It downloads a single `.Rmd` file, which describes what you did and
holds the `nicheR` calls with your parameters filled in, so it works
as a starting script rather than only as a description of what you clicked.
The app does not run the script for you. Knit the file, or run its chunks from
the console, to get the HTML with the results and figures.

The report follows the same four steps as the app. Each section lists the
parameters you used, the objects that resulted, and the code that would produce
them from the console.


<!-- SCREENSHOT: -->
<img src='figures/shiny_app_figures/Slide20.png' 
align='center' 
height='100%' 
width='100%'/>

<br>


## What the report contains depends on your path

Sections appear only when the objects they describe exist. Skipping bias, or
working without geography, does not leave an empty heading in the report; the
section is simply not written. The same rule applies within a section, so a
Generate section built from three record sets documents three, not a
placeholder for every option you did not use.

| How you started | Sections written |
|---|---|
| Rasters, or a CSV with gridded coordinates | Build, Predict, Bias, Generate |
| The same, with **Skip bias** | Build, Predict, Generate |
| CSV with no usable coordinates | Build, Predict, Generate, with no geographic figures |
| Virtual mode | Build, Generate |

**Virtual mode** produces the shortest report. There is no prediction and no
bias surface to describe, and the Generate section documents `virtual_data()`
rather than `sample_data()`, so the parameters recorded are truncation and point
distribution rather than sampling strategy and weighting method. Every figure is
in environmental space.

**A CSV without coordinates** still gives you Build and Predict, since
suitability values do not require geography, but the report carries no maps and
no Bias section. This matches what the app itself allows.

**Bias** is reported per composite surface. The layers you uploaded, their
assigned directions, the NA handling rule, and the resulting formula are all
recorded, and the Generate section cross-references which record sets came
from a biased layer and which did not.

## File paths

The report records the name of every file you uploaded, but not a working path
to it. A browser sends only the name of a file, never the folder it came from,
so the script cannot know where your copy lives. It reads each file by name from
a folder called `data_dir`, which is declared once near the top of the script.
Set it to the folder holding your files and the script runs as written. If you
save the `.Rmd` in that same folder, you can knit it without changing anything.

That first chunk also checks that every file is there, and stops with the names
of any it can't find. If one file name is read in more than one step, for
example as background data and as a bias layer, the script says so in a
comment, because two different files can't share a name in one folder.

The app does not keep copies of your uploads, so a report from a reloaded
session is the same as one from the session that made it. A session built
on the example data needs no folder at all, since those layers ship with the
package and the report writes a `system.file()` call for them.

Saving the session with the **Save** button is the reliable way to preserve
state. The report preserves the reasoning; the `.rds` preserves the objects.
